variants.note: before a vowel sound, as in *the apple*; also the strong form in American English
the strong form, when the word is stressed or said alone

pronunciation.notes: **The** is normally unstressed: *ðə* before a consonant sound (*the car*, *the university*) and *ði* before a vowel sound (*the apple*, *the hour*). The strong form, *ði* in American and *ðiː* in British English, is used when the word is stressed or said alone.

core_idea: **The** points to a particular person or thing, one that the listener or reader can tell from all the others.

senses.definition: used before a noun to show that the listener or reader knows which person or thing is meant
senses.explanation: The person or thing is known because it was mentioned before (*I bought a coat and a hat; the hat was cheap*), because it is clear from the situation (*Could you close the door?*), or because the words after the noun say which one (*the book I lent you*).

examples.text: I bought a coat and a hat. The hat was cheap.
Could you close the door?
Where is the book I lent you?
examples.note: made clear by the words after the noun

examples.text: The children are asleep at last.

compare.note: **a** or **an** is used when the listener does not yet know which one is meant, or when it does not matter which

subsenses.definition: used instead of **my**, **your**, **his**, and so on before a part of the body, especially after a preposition

examples.text: The ball hit him on the head.
She took the child by the hand.
He looked me in the eye and said no.

senses.definition: used before a noun for something of which there is only one, or only one that matters to the people talking
senses.explanation: There is no need to say which one: *the sun*, *the sky*, *the sea*, *the world*. In the same way people say *the doctor*, *the station*, *the government*, or *the news*, meaning the one in their own life or town.

examples.text: The moon was very bright last night.
We sat on the beach and watched the sea.
I have to go to the doctor tomorrow.
What did it say on the news?

senses.definition: used before a singular noun to talk about every member of a kind of thing
senses.explanation: This use is common in writing and in general statements about animals, machines, and instruments: *the tiger*, *the computer*, *the piano*. In everyday speech a plural noun with no article is more usual: *Bicycles are cheap*; *computers have changed the way we work*. For a musical instrument, **the** is the normal choice: *play the piano*.

examples.text: The bicycle is a cheap way to get around.
The computer has changed the way we work.
Yuki is learning to play the piano.
Do you play the guitar?

subsenses.definition: used before an adjective to mean all the people of that kind
subsenses.explanation: **The** plus an adjective takes a plural verb: *the poor are*, not *the poor is*.

examples.text: The rich are getting richer.
The hospital cares for the sick and the elderly.
There are programs to help the unemployed.

senses.definition: used before words such as **best**, **biggest**, **first**, **second**, **only**, **same**, **next**, and **last**, which pick out one thing from all the others
senses.explanation: These words leave only one possible choice, so **the** goes with them: *the best day*, *the first time*, *the same thing*. **Next** and **last** take **the** when they mean the one after or before in a series, but not in *next week* or *last year*.

examples.text: This is the best coffee I have ever had.
Kim was the first person to arrive.
Sara is the only one who knows the answer.
We took the same bus home.

senses.definition: used before two words such as **more**, **less**, or **bigger**, in pairs, to say that as one thing changes, another changes with it
senses.explanation: Both halves begin with **the** plus a word such as **more** or **bigger**, and the second half gives the result: *The more I read, the less I understand*. The second half is often shortened: *The sooner, the better*.

examples.text: The more you practice, the easier it gets.
The sooner we leave, the better.
The bigger the box, the more it costs to send.

senses.definition: used after **by** before a unit of measurement to say how something is counted, sold, or paid for

examples.text: The workers are paid by the hour.
Apples are sold by the kilo at the market.
You can rent a boat by the day.

senses.definition: used with strong stress before a noun to say that this is the best known or most important one of its kind
senses.explanation: Here **the** is said with stress, *ði* in American English and *ðiː* in British English, and in print it is often in italics. It says that everyone knows or wants this one: *the place to eat*, *the person to ask*.

examples.text: Their cafe has become the place to meet in our neighborhood.
She is the person to ask about old films.
It was the party of the year.

usage_note: **The** is used before the names of rivers, seas, oceans, deserts, groups of islands or mountains, and countries whose names are plural or contain a noun such as **republic** or **kingdom**. Most other names, of people, cities, countries, streets, and single lakes or mountains, take no article.

learner_errors.note: **Nature**, **life**, **music**, and other uncountable nouns take no article when they mean the thing in general.

learner_errors.incorrect: I like the music very much.
learner_errors.note: With **the**, the sentence means a particular piece of music that both people know about; for music in general, use no article.
A singular countable noun needs a determiner, and the listener knows which bathroom is meant.

adaptation.semantic: Languages with articles do not all use them where English does. Many put an article before an abstract or general noun (*life*, *music*, *nature*) where English has none, and some use one before a name or a possessed noun. Translate **the** by asking whether the listener can already tell which one is meant.
adaptation.grammar: Many languages have no article, and learners from them leave **the** out or add it where English has none. A singular countable noun always needs some determiner. Use **the** when both speaker and listener know which one is meant; use no article for a plural or uncountable noun taken in general.
adaptation.pronunciation: Weak forms: *ðə* before a consonant sound and *ði* before a vowel sound: *the apple*, *the hour* (the **h** is silent). The choice depends on the sound, not the letter: *the university* takes *ðə* because it begins with a **y** sound. The strong form is used only for stress.
